question: Last year, 2 042 organ donations were made in Italy, while the number of transplants reached 4 462. A total of 13.5 million citizens have recorded their decision to consent to organ donation on the national transplant information system.

Yet, despite the fact that donation rates are continuously rising across Europe, the existing EU legislation on donation and on the exchange of human organs between Member States dates back to 2010 and 2012 respectively.

The sector faces many challenges, from countries having different cultural approaches to donation to there being a lack of proper and comprehensive information on donation and, above all, adequate and effective cooperation between Member States. Meanwhile, more than 50 000 EU citizens are waiting for a transplant. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission plan in the near future to set up an integration system for organ donations between Member States?
Will it introduce funding for the national bodies that have for years been trying to get things to progress in this area?
Does it not see a need to establish a harmonised awareness-raising programme to encourage more people to opt in to being donors in the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2024) The Commission appreciates the Honourable Member’s interest in the field of organ transplantation and in the need to further strengthen transplant programmes in the EU. As the Commission pointed out in its reply to written question E-002498/20211 and supplements the actions of the Member States (Article 6 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (TFEU)).

The EU’s competence in the field of public health is limited under Article 168 TFEU and as regards organs covers setting standards for quality and safety (Article 168(4)(a) TFEU) without affecting national provisions on the donation or medical use of organs (Article 168(7) TFEU). The organisation of transplant care does not fall under the EU competence but under the competence of the Member States.

It is therefore not possible for the Commission to engage in organisational actions to build such cross-national integration or to harmonize awareness building programmes that are organised by Member States and tailored to their different national populations and preferences.
The EU however brings national competent authorities together and supports the sector through EU4Health funded actions, in particular to exchange good national practices, such as the BRAVEST action3.

The Commission also underlines that several actions developed under the EU Action Plan on Organ Donation and Transplantation 2009-2015 are still relevant while Member States implement organisational improvement in their national transplant systems.
